title: Practice GED Form 10 — Reasoning Through Language Arts

stimuli.title: Racing the Wire: The Pony Express and the Telegraph
stimuli.html:
[1] In the spring of 1860, California had a problem. It had become a state ten years earlier, and hundreds of thousands of people had moved there since the Gold Rush. Yet news from the East still traveled at the speed of a ship or a stagecoach. A letter mailed in New York might go by steamship to Panama, cross the isthmus by train, and sail north to San Francisco, a trip of roughly three to four weeks. Overland stagecoaches were not much faster. With the nation sliding toward civil war, Californians wanted news from the East, and they wanted it quickly.

[2] A freight company owned by William Russell, Alexander Majors, and William Waddell believed it had an answer. On April 3, 1860, a rider left St. Joseph, Missouri, carrying a leather pouch of letters west toward Sacramento, California, nearly 2,000 miles away. The plan depended on speed and relays. Stations were built every 10 to 15 miles along the route. At each one, a rider leaped from a tired horse onto a fresh one, often in under two minutes, and galloped on. After riding about 75 to 100 miles, he handed the mail to a new rider. Working day and night, the system could move a letter across the continent in about ten days.

[3] Speed came at a high price. Riders had to be young, light, and willing to cross deserts and mountain passes alone, sometimes through snow or blistering heat. The company bought hundreds of horses and paid for food, station keepers, and supplies across some of the most remote country in North America. To cover these costs, it charged $5 for every half ounce of mail, at a time when many workers earned about a dollar a day. Ordinary families rarely used the service. Most customers were newspapers, banks, merchants, and government offices that needed information before their competitors did.

[4] The Pony Express also worked alongside a faster technology. Telegraph lines, which sent coded electrical signals over wire almost instantly, already ran from the East as far west as Nebraska and from California east into what is now Nevada. Between those points lay a gap of more than a thousand miles with no wire at all. A message could be telegraphed to the end of one line, carried across the gap by riders, and telegraphed again from the other end. In March 1861, riders crossed that gap with the text of President Abraham Lincoln’s first inaugural address in record time, by most accounts about seven days and seventeen hours.

[5] That partnership carried the seeds of the Pony Express’s end. In June 1860, Congress had passed the Pacific Telegraph Act, which offered government money to build a line connecting the two coasts. Crews working from the east and from the west raced across plains and deserts, setting poles and stringing wire. Every mile they finished made the riders’ route shorter. On October 24, 1861, the two lines met in Salt Lake City, and messages could flash across the continent in minutes. Two days later, the Pony Express announced that it would stop carrying mail. The last pouches finished their journeys in November.

[6] The Pony Express had lasted about eighteen months. It never made a profit. Even after the price was lowered to $1 per half ounce, the company lost large sums of money, and its owners’ freight business soon collapsed under its debts. Judged as a business, it was a failure.

[7] Yet few businesses that lasted so briefly are remembered so well. Part of the reason is legend. Dime novels and, later, traveling Wild West shows turned the riders into heroes. William “Buffalo Bill” Cody later claimed that he had ridden for the Pony Express as a teenager, a story many historians doubt because little evidence from the time supports it. But the Pony Express also marks a real turning point. Its riders represented about the fastest that a message could travel when someone had to carry it. The telegraph that replaced them opened an age in which information no longer needed a messenger at all.
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.

stimuli.title: Red Water
stimuli.html:
[1] The flood went onto the bog at midnight, and by five in the morning the Haskell bog was a black lake with a rim of frost around it. Tess stood on the dike in her grandfather’s waders, which came up past her ribs, and watched her breath drift over water that hid six acres of vines and every berry they had made since spring.

[2] “You know the speed,” her grandfather said from the truck. His right arm was in a sling, strapped tight against his chest where the doctor had put it after he fell from the pump-house ladder. “Slow. Slower than you want. The reel does the work.”

[3] “I know.” She had known since she was eight, when he first let her sit beside him on the water reel and steer it with her hands under his. She had also known, since August, that she would not be here next October. The acceptance letter from the nursing program in Baltimore was folded into the back of the phone case in her pocket, and she had not yet found the right morning to tell him. This was not that morning.

[4] She climbed down into the water. The cold went through the rubber as if the rubber were not there. The water reel waited at the edge of the bog, its paddle wheel lifted clear of the surface. She started the engine, lowered the wheel, and eased forward.

[5] At first there was only black water churning white. Then the berries began to rise. They came up one at a time, then by the dozen, then all at once, knocked loose from the vines by the beating paddles and floating because each berry held tiny pockets of air inside it. By the time she reached the far ditch, a red stripe trailed behind her across the dark bog, exactly the width of the reel and as straight as a ruled line on paper.

[6] She turned and came back. Another stripe. Another. Behind her the bog filled in with red, and when the sun cleared the pines it lit the surface until it looked less like fruit than like something poured.

[7] On the dike, her grandfather had gotten out of the truck. He did not shout corrections. He did not wave her slower. He stood with his good hand in his coat pocket and watched the way he watched weather, as if it were something a person could learn only by keeping still.

[8] When the last row was done, she shut off the engine, and in the sudden quiet she could hear the berries bumping softly against one another, a sound like a crowd whispering in another room. She waded to the dike. Her legs had stopped feeling the cold an hour ago.

[9] “Straight rows,” he said.

[10] “You taught me.”

[11] “I taught your father too.” He looked out at the red water. “His rows wandered like a dog off its leash. He never cared for any of this, and that was all right. Fields don’t need everybody. They just need somebody, for a while.” He was quiet a moment. “You’ll be somebody for a while, Tess. That’s enough.”

[12] She understood then that he already knew about the letter, about Baltimore, maybe about all of it. Maybe her mother had told him. Maybe he had simply watched her the way he watched the bog. She opened her mouth to explain, and he shook his head once, the way he did when a pump was running fine and there was no need to touch it.

[13] Behind them the crew was dragging the long floating booms into place to sweep the berries toward the pump. Tess picked up the end of a boom line. Her grandfather took the other end in his one good hand, and together, slowly, slower than she wanted, they began to pull the red water in.
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.

stimuli.title: Trade the Turf: Native Plants Make Sense for Our Town
stimuli.html:
Across the United States, lawns cover a remarkable amount of land. A NASA-funded study published in 2005 estimated that turf grass covered about 40 million acres of the country, which would make it, by area, the largest irrigated crop in the nation. Keeping that grass green takes water. According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, landscape irrigation accounts for nearly one-third of all residential water use nationwide. Towns that face summer water shortages should encourage homeowners to replace part of their lawns with native plants, and the most effective tool is a simple, voluntary rebate.

Native plants are species that grew in a region before modern development, so they are adapted to its rainfall and soil. Once established, usually after one or two growing seasons, many need little watering beyond what falls from the sky.

Our neighbors have already tested this idea. In 2019, the town of Ashby Falls began paying homeowners $1 for every square foot of lawn they replaced with native plantings. The town’s water utility tracked the 312 households that took part. Over the next three summers, those homes used an average of 24 percent less water from June through August than they had before converting. A comparison group of similar households that kept their lawns showed almost no change. The program cost Ashby Falls about $410,000, far less than the estimated $1.2 million needed to expand its water treatment plant, an expansion the town has now postponed.

The benefits go beyond water. Native flowering plants feed bees, butterflies, and birds that cannot survive on grass alone. When biologists from a nearby state university surveyed 40 yards in Ashby Falls in 2022, they found about three times as many species of native bees in converted yards as in traditional lawns.

Some residents worry that native yards look messy or will lower property values. These concerns deserve a response, and good programs provide one. Ashby Falls offers free planting designs and requires a tidy border along sidewalks. Most importantly, no one is forced to take part. Homeowners who love their grass can keep every blade of it.

A rebate program is inexpensive, voluntary, and proven. It saves water when water is scarce and gives wildlife a place to live. Our town should adopt one this year.
stimuli.source: By Dr. Maya Okafor-Lindqvist, water resources engineer. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.

stimuli.title: Leave Lawns to the People Who Own Them
stimuli.html:
Every few years, town hall comes up with a new idea about how homeowners should use their own property. The latest proposal is to pay people to tear out their lawns and plant “native” gardens. I have cut grass in this town for twenty-two years, and I can tell you that this plan is a mistake.

First, a lawn is part of the American way of life. Generations of families have played catch, hosted barbecues, and watched their children take first steps on green grass. Replacing that with tall weeds and wildflowers changes the character of a neighborhood, and nobody I know wants that.

Second, native yards bring problems that supporters do not mention. Tall plants give ticks, snakes, and rodents a place to hide. One of my customers who tried a wildflower bed told me she saw more mice that summer than ever before. Studies show that overgrown yards attract pests, and no rebate will pay the exterminator.

Third, the rebates are not as generous as they sound. Removing grass, preparing soil, and buying plants can cost homeowners several dollars per square foot, far more than a typical rebate covers. New plantings also need regular watering for their first season or two, so the savings do not appear right away. That means the program will mostly help homeowners who already have money to spare, using tax dollars collected from everyone.

Finally, we should remember where programs like this lead. Today the rebate is voluntary. Tomorrow, the town will be fining people whose grass is too green. Once government starts deciding what grows in your yard, there is no stopping point.

Lawn care also supports good local jobs. My company employs eleven people, and businesses like mine buy equipment, fuel, and supplies right here in town. If the town wants to save water, it can remind residents to water early in the morning. It should leave lawns, and the choice of what to plant, to the people who own them.
stimuli.source: By Gary Petrakis, owner of Petrakis Lawn & Landscape. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.

stimuli.title: Measuring the Shaking: How Scientists Size Up Earthquakes
stimuli.html:
[1] Within minutes of a large earthquake, news reports announce a single number: magnitude 6.4, or magnitude 7.1. That number looks simple, but it is the product of nearly a century of scientific work, and the scale behind it has changed more than most people realize.

[2] Earthquakes are recorded by instruments called seismometers, which detect vibrations as seismic waves travel through the ground. The record a seismometer produces, called a seismogram, shows those waves as a line that swings back and forth. The larger the swings, the stronger the shaking at that instrument. Today, thousands of seismometers around the world send data to scientists continuously, allowing them to locate an earthquake and estimate its size within minutes.

[3] In 1935, seismologist Charles Richter, working with his colleague Beno Gutenberg in California, developed a way to compare earthquakes using a single number. Richter’s method measured the height, or amplitude, of the largest wave recorded on a particular type of seismometer, adjusted for the instrument’s distance from the earthquake. Because earthquakes vary so enormously in size, Richter made his scale logarithmic: each increase of one whole number represents a tenfold increase in the amplitude of the recorded waves. In terms of energy released, each one-step increase means about 32 times more energy. A magnitude 6 earthquake therefore releases roughly 1,000 times as much energy as a magnitude 4.

[4] The Richter scale was a breakthrough, but it had limits. It was designed for earthquakes in Southern California, measured on one kind of instrument at fairly close distances. More importantly, it did not work well for the largest earthquakes. Above about magnitude 7, the method began to underestimate an earthquake’s size, because the waves it measured stopped growing as quickly as the earthquakes themselves did. As a result, two very large earthquakes could receive similar Richter numbers even if one was far more powerful than the other.

[5] To solve this problem, seismologists Thomas Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori introduced the moment magnitude scale in 1979. Instead of relying on the height of a single wave, moment magnitude is based on the physical size of the earthquake itself: how stiff the rock is, how large an area of the fault slipped, and how far the two sides of the fault moved. Because it measures the event directly rather than one of its effects, moment magnitude works for earthquakes of every size, anywhere in the world. Today, moment magnitude has replaced the Richter scale for most measurements, and it is the standard the U.S. Geological Survey uses for large earthquakes. Its numbers were designed to match Richter values for moderate earthquakes, which is one reason news reports sometimes still mention “the Richter scale” even when a figure actually comes from moment magnitude.

[6] Magnitude, however, answers only one question: how big was the earthquake? It does not say how strongly the ground shook in a particular town. For that, scientists use intensity, which in the United States is most often measured with the Modified Mercalli Intensity scale. Intensity is written in Roman numerals, from I (not felt) to XII (extreme destruction), and it is based on what people felt and what happened to buildings and the landscape. A single earthquake has one magnitude, but it produces many intensity values, usually highest near the source and lower farther away. Local conditions matter too: loose, soft soil can make shaking stronger than it is on solid rock at the same distance.

[7] Scientists now gather intensity information in a way Richter could never have imagined. After an earthquake, members of the public can report what they felt through the U.S. Geological Survey’s online “Did You Feel It?” survey. Thousands of responses can arrive within an hour, producing a map of shaking that helps emergency managers decide where help may be needed first.

[8] Measuring earthquakes precisely cannot prevent them. But accurate numbers help engineers design stronger buildings, help communities understand their risk, and help responders act quickly when the ground begins to move.
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.

stimuli.title: Missed Delivery Credit: Frequently Asked Questions
stimuli.html:
Fieldstone Meal Kits
Missed Delivery Credit: Frequently Asked Questions

Who is eligible?
Any customer whose box was scheduled for delivery between March 9 and March 13 and was canceled by Fieldstone is eligible. Customers who chose to skip that week were not charged and are not eligible.

How much is the credit, and when will I receive it?
The credit equals the full price of the canceled box, including shipping. It will be added to your account automatically by March 20. You do not need to contact us.

How do I use the credit?
The credit is applied automatically to your next box. If the credit is larger than the price of that box, the remaining balance carries over to your following orders until it is used up. Credits expire 90 days after they are issued. If your subscription is paused, the 90 days do not begin until you resume deliveries.

Can I get a refund instead?
Yes. You may choose a refund to your original payment method instead of a credit. Refund requests must be made by March 31. To request a refund:

  1. Log in to your account at the Fieldstone website.
  2. Open Order History and select the canceled box.
  3. Click Request Refund.
  4. Watch for a confirmation email, which will arrive within 24 hours.

Refunds appear on your statement within 5 to 7 business days after you receive the confirmation email. When you request a refund, the credit for that box is removed from your account. You cannot receive both a credit and a refund for the same box.

I canceled my subscription. What happens to my credit?
Because a credit cannot be used without a subscription, we will automatically refund the value of your canceled box to your original payment method by March 31. No action is needed.

My box arrived during that week, but some items were damaged. Am I covered?
Boxes that were delivered that week were shipped from our other distribution centers and are not part of this credit. To report damaged or missing items, use the Report a Problem button in Order History within 7 days of delivery and include a photo. You will receive a credit for the affected items.
stimuli.source: Original workplace document written for KCE GED Prep.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: The Pony Express failed because its riders could not safely cross the mountains in winter.
Although the Pony Express was short-lived and unprofitable, it filled a gap in communication until the telegraph replaced it and changed how information traveled.
The telegraph was invented in 1861 so that the government would no longer need to pay Pony Express riders.
The Pony Express was the main way that California families exchanged letters with relatives in the East.
items.explain:
The passage describes the slow mail that created a need for speed (paragraph 1), how the Pony Express worked and what it cost (paragraphs 2–3), how it carried messages across the gap between telegraph lines (paragraph 4), how the completed telegraph ended it (paragraph 5), its financial failure (paragraph 6), and why it still matters as a turning point (paragraph 7).

The passage never blames winter weather for its end. Telegraph lines already existed before 1861 (paragraph 4); 1861 is when the coast-to-coast line was completed. Paragraph 3 says ordinary families rarely used the service.
why: The passage never blames winter weather. Paragraph 5 says the completed telegraph ended the service, and paragraph 6 says it lost money.
Paragraph 4 says telegraph lines already ran partway across the country before 1861; 1861 is when the coast-to-coast line was finished, not when the telegraph was invented.
Paragraph 3 says "Ordinary families rarely used the service"; most customers were newspapers, banks, merchants, and government offices.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 1?
options: to compare the cost of sending mail by ship with the cost of sending it by stagecoach
to describe how the Gold Rush brought hundreds of thousands of people to California
to explain the problem of slow communication that the Pony Express was created to solve
to argue that California should have waited longer before becoming a state
items.explain:
Paragraph 1 shows that news from the East took “roughly three to four weeks” to reach California and that Californians “wanted it quickly.” Paragraph 2 then begins, “A freight company … believed it had an answer,” so paragraph 1 sets up the problem.

The paragraph gives travel times, not costs. The Gold Rush is mentioned only to explain why so many people lived in California, and the author never questions statehood.
why: Paragraph 1 gives travel times ("three to four weeks"), not costs. Its job is to set up the problem of slow news.
The Gold Rush is mentioned only to explain why so many people lived in California. The paragraph's focus is how slowly news reached them.
The author never questions California's statehood. Paragraph 1 sets up the slow-news problem that paragraph 2 says the company "had an answer" for.

items.prompt: Paragraph 3 is shown below. Click the sentence that best explains who used the Pony Express most and why they were willing to pay for it.
spans: Speed came at a high price.
Riders had to be young, light, and willing to cross deserts and mountain passes alone, sometimes through snow or blistering heat.
The company bought hundreds of horses and paid for food, station keepers, and supplies across some of the most remote country in North America.
To cover these costs, it charged $5 for every half ounce of mail, at a time when many workers earned about a dollar a day.
Ordinary families rarely used the service.
Most customers were newspapers, banks, merchants, and government offices that needed information before their competitors did.
items.explain:
The last sentence names the main customers (“newspapers, banks, merchants, and government offices”) and gives their reason: they “needed information before their competitors did.”

The sentence about the $5 price explains the cost, and “Ordinary families rarely used the service” tells who did not use it, but neither one identifies the main customers and their reason.
items.why: A common wrong click is "Ordinary families rarely used the service" or the $5 price sentence. Those tell who did not use it and what it cost; only the last sentence names the main customers and their reason: they "needed information before their competitors did."

items.prompt: According to the passage, how did the building of the coast-to-coast telegraph line affect the Pony Express before the line was finished?
options: Riders were hired to help set poles and string wire.
Riders had to travel farther to reach the ends of the telegraph lines.
The company raised its price to pay for the new technology.
Each new section of wire made the distance the riders had to cover shorter.
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 says, “Every mile they finished made the riders’ route shorter.” Because messages were telegraphed to the end of each line and carried across the gap (paragraph 4), the gap shrank as the lines grew.

The distance became shorter, not longer. The price was lowered, not raised (paragraph 6), and the passage says nothing about riders building the line.
why: The passage never says riders built the line; paragraph 5 describes separate crews setting poles and stringing wire.
The distance got shorter, not longer: paragraph 5 says, "Every mile they finished made the riders' route shorter."
Paragraph 6 says the price was lowered to $1, not raised, and nothing links prices to the new technology.

items.prompt: Put these events from the passage in the order in which they happened. Drag each event into the correct position.
choices: The Pony Express announces that it will stop carrying mail.
Congress passes the Pacific Telegraph Act.
Riders carry Lincoln’s first inaugural address across the gap between telegraph lines.
The first rider leaves St. Joseph, Missouri.
The eastern and western telegraph lines meet in Salt Lake City.
items.explain:
(1) The first rider left on April 3, 1860 (paragraph 2). (2) Congress passed the Pacific Telegraph Act in June 1860 (paragraph 5). (3) Riders carried Lincoln’s address in March 1861 (paragraph 4). (4) The lines met on October 24, 1861 (paragraph 5). (5) The Pony Express announced its end two days later (paragraph 5).

Note that the Telegraph Act is described in paragraph 5, after the 1861 inaugural address, but the dates show it came first.
items.why: The most common error is placing the Pacific Telegraph Act after Lincoln's address because paragraph 5 describes it later. Use the dates: the Act passed in June 1860, after the first ride in April 1860 but before the March 1861 address.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the author writes, “That partnership carried the seeds of the Pony Express’s end.” What does this sentence mean?
options: The cooperation between the riders and the telegraph contained the beginning of what would eventually put the riders out of business.
The Pony Express shipped seeds and supplies to the telegraph crews working in the desert.
The partnership with the telegraph delayed the end of the Pony Express by several years.
The Pony Express ended because the telegraph companies refused to work with it.
items.explain:
Seeds are the small beginnings of something that grows later. The Pony Express worked with the telegraph by carrying messages between the ends of the lines (paragraph 4), but the same telegraph kept growing until it closed the gap and ended the need for riders (paragraph 5).

The phrase is figurative; no actual seeds are involved. The passage does not say the partnership delayed the end or that the telegraph companies refused to cooperate.
why: "Seeds" is figurative here; no actual seeds were shipped. It means the partnership held the small beginning of the service's end.
Paragraph 5 says the growing telegraph shortened the riders' route and ended the service within months of the lines meeting; it did not delay the end by years.
The passage says the riders and telegraph worked together (paragraph 4). The service ended because the telegraph was completed, not because the companies refused to cooperate.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 7, which conclusion about how the Pony Express is remembered is best supported?
options: It is remembered mainly because it earned large profits for its owners.
Historians agree that Buffalo Bill Cody was its most famous rider.
Its fame rests partly on popular stories that are exaggerated or not supported by evidence.
Dime novels were an accurate record of the riders’ daily lives.
items.explain:
Paragraph 7 says “Part of the reason is legend,” that dime novels and Wild West shows “turned the riders into heroes,” and that many historians doubt Cody’s claim “because little evidence from the time supports it.” Together these details show that some of its fame comes from stories rather than proven facts.

Paragraph 6 says it “never made a profit.” Historians doubt, rather than agree with, Cody’s story, and nothing suggests dime novels were accurate records.
why: Paragraph 6 says the Pony Express "never made a profit," so profit cannot be why it is remembered.
Paragraph 7 says many historians doubt Cody's claim because "little evidence from the time supports it." They do not agree he was its most famous rider.
Paragraph 7 says dime novels "turned the riders into heroes," which is legend-making, not accurate record keeping.

items.prompt: The author states, “Judged as a business, it was a failure.” Which details from the passage support this statement? Select two answers.
options: The company lost large sums of money even after it lowered its price.
Riders changed horses at stations every 10 to 15 miles.
The owners’ freight business soon collapsed under its debts.
Riders carried Lincoln’s inaugural address in record time.
Dime novels and Wild West shows turned the riders into heroes.
items.explain:
Paragraph 6 explains the financial failure: even with a lower price, “the company lost large sums of money,” and the owners’ freight business “soon collapsed under its debts.”

The relay stations explain how the system worked, the record ride shows its success at speed, and the dime novels explain its fame. None of these shows a business failure.
why: The relay stations explain how the system worked, not whether it made money.
The record ride shows the service's speed, which is a success, not a business failure.
The dime novels explain the service's fame, not its finances.

items.prompt: What can the reader infer about Tess from paragraph 3?
options: She does not know what speed to use when running the water reel.
She has made a decision about her future that she expects will be hard to share with her grandfather.
She is angry that her grandfather fell from the pump-house ladder.
She has decided to turn down the nursing program so she can stay on the bog.
items.explain:
Tess has known “since August” that she “would not be here next October,” she keeps the acceptance letter hidden in her phone case, and she “had not yet found the right morning to tell him.” Waiting for the “right morning” shows she expects the news to be difficult for him.

Nothing suggests she is angry or that she is turning the program down; the letter is still with her and she plans to leave. Her answer, “I know,” and her years of steering the reel since she was eight show she knows the speed.
why: She answers "I know" and has steered the reel since she was eight, so she knows the speed.
Nothing in paragraph 3 shows anger about his fall. Her feelings there are about the news she has not yet shared.
The acceptance letter is still in her phone case, and she plans not to be there next October. Nothing suggests she is turning the program down.

items.prompt: In paragraph 8, the sound of the floating berries is compared to “a crowd whispering in another room.” What does this comparison suggest about the sound?
options: It is loud and alarming, like a warning of trouble.
It is soft and steady, made of many small noises blending together.
It comes from the crew members who are talking about Tess.
It is the sound of the berries being crushed by the paddles.
items.explain:
A crowd whispering in another room is quiet, constant, and made up of many separate voices that blend together, just like thousands of berries “bumping softly against one another” in “the sudden quiet” after the engine stops.

“Softly” rules out a loud sound. The crowd is a comparison, not real people talking, and the engine is already off, so the paddles are not crushing anything.
why: The berries are "bumping softly" in "the sudden quiet," and a whisper is soft, so the sound is not loud or alarming.
The crowd is a comparison, not real people. The sound comes from the berries bumping against each other.
The engine is already off when she hears the sound, so the paddles are not crushing anything; the berries are floating and bumping softly.

items.prompt: What does paragraph 7 reveal about Tess’s grandfather?
options: He is too tired from his injury to pay attention to the harvest.
He is disappointed in how Tess is running the water reel.
He trusts Tess’s skill and watches patiently instead of directing her.
He does not understand how the new water reel works.
items.explain:
Paragraph 7 says he “did not shout corrections” and “did not wave her slower.” He watches quietly, “as if it were something a person could learn only by keeping still.” He gives no instructions because he trusts her work.

He has gotten out of the truck to watch closely, so he is paying attention. His later comment, “Straight rows,” is praise, not disappointment, and he taught Tess to run the reel, so he understands it.
why: He has gotten out of the truck to watch closely, so he is paying attention, not too tired.
He does not correct her, and his later comment, "Straight rows," is praise, not disappointment.
He taught Tess to run the reel and told her "The reel does the work," so he understands it well.

items.prompt: In paragraph 11, the grandfather says, “Fields don’t need everybody. They just need somebody, for a while.” What does he most likely mean?
options: The bog needs more workers than the family can provide.
Tess’s father should come back and take over the bog.
Farm work is so simple that anyone can learn it in a short time.
Tess does not have to give her whole life to the bog; caring for it well for a time is enough.
items.explain:
He has just said that Tess’s father “never cared for any of this, and that was all right.” He then tells Tess, “You’ll be somebody for a while, Tess. That’s enough.” In paragraph 12 Tess realizes he already knows about Baltimore. He is telling her that her leaving is acceptable and her help now still matters.

He does not ask for more workers or for her father to return; he says it was “all right” that her father did not care for the work. The story shows the work takes years to learn, so he is not calling it simple.
why: He says fields need only "somebody, for a while," which is the opposite of asking for more workers.
He says it was "all right" that Tess's father never cared for the work, so he is not asking the father to return.
The story shows the skill takes years (she learned at eight), so he is not calling the work simple. He is talking about who must care for the bog, and for how long.

items.prompt: Paragraph 12 is shown below. Click the sentence in which the grandfather signals, without words, that Tess does not need to explain her plans.
spans: She understood then that he already knew about the letter, about Baltimore, maybe about all of it.
Maybe her mother had told him.
Maybe he had simply watched her the way he watched the bog.
She opened her mouth to explain, and he shook his head once, the way he did when a pump was running fine and there was no need to touch it.
items.explain:
When Tess “opened her mouth to explain,” the grandfather “shook his head once, the way he did when a pump was running fine and there was no need to touch it.” His gesture tells her that nothing needs fixing or explaining.

The first three sentences show what Tess realizes and guesses about how he found out, but they do not show his response to her.
items.why: A common wrong click is the first sentence, where Tess realizes he knows. That sentence shows her thought, not his signal; his wordless signal is shaking his head once, "the way he did when a pump was running fine."

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: Young people should follow family tradition instead of their own plans.
Hard work on a farm always leads to financial success.
Loving a place does not require staying forever; caring for it well for a time can be enough.
Machines have made farm work easier than it was in the past.
items.explain:
Tess plans to leave for nursing school, yet she runs the harvest with care, and her grandfather tells her, “You’ll be somebody for a while, Tess. That’s enough.” The story ends with the two of them working together, showing that her care for the bog is real even though she will leave.

The grandfather accepts that Tess and her father follow their own paths, which contradicts the idea that young people should follow family tradition instead of their own plans. Money is never discussed, and the water reel is a detail of the setting, not the story’s message.
why: The grandfather accepts that Tess and her father follow their own paths ("that was all right"), so the story does not say tradition should come first.
Money is never discussed in the story, so it says nothing about farm work leading to financial success.
The water reel is a detail of the setting. The story's message is about Tess's relationship with the bog and her grandfather, not machines.

items.prompt: Which details from the story best show that Tess runs the water reel skillfully? Select two answers.
options: Her grandfather’s waders come up past her ribs.
The red stripe behind her is “as straight as a ruled line on paper.”
Her legs stop feeling the cold after an hour.
Her grandfather comments, “Straight rows.”
The crew drags floating booms into place to sweep the berries toward the pump.
The acceptance letter is folded into the back of her phone case.
items.explain:
A stripe “as straight as a ruled line on paper” (paragraph 5) shows careful, steady control of the reel, and her grandfather’s praise, “Straight rows” (paragraph 9), confirms her skill, especially since he compares it with her father’s rows that “wandered like a dog off its leash.”

The waders, the cold, the crew’s booms, and the letter describe the setting, her discomfort, or her plans, not her skill.
why: The oversized waders describe what she is wearing, not how well she runs the reel.
Her numb legs show how cold and long the work was, not her skill.
The crew's booms are the next step of the harvest and show nothing about Tess's skill with the reel.
The letter relates to her future plans, not to how she runs the reel.

items.prompt: The story ends with Tess and her grandfather pulling the boom line “slowly, slower than she wanted.” How does this ending connect to the beginning of the story?
options: It echoes the grandfather’s advice in paragraph 2, suggesting that Tess now shares his patient way of working with him.
It shows that Tess has forgotten the instructions her grandfather gave her in paragraph 2.
It reveals that the water reel has broken down and must be pulled by hand.
It suggests that Tess has changed her mind and will stay on the bog.
items.explain:
In paragraph 2 the grandfather tells her, “Slow. Slower than you want.” The final sentence repeats that phrase as the two of them work together, which shows Tess accepting his patient approach and sharing a moment with him.

Repeating his words shows she remembers his advice, not that she forgot it. The reel finished its work; pulling the booms is the next step of the harvest. Nothing in the ending says Tess will stay; her grandfather has just accepted that she will leave.
why: Repeating "slower than she wanted" shows she remembers and now shares his advice from paragraph 2; she has not forgotten it.
The reel already finished its work; paragraph 13 describes the next step of the harvest, pulling the booms.
Nothing in the ending says Tess will stay. Her grandfather has just accepted that she is leaving.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the training manual. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The first few minutes of a guest’s stay {{0}} the tone for the entire visit.”

options: sets
set
is setting
has set
why: Sets agrees with "stay," but the subject is minutes, which is plural. Use set.
Is setting is singular and agrees with "stay." The plural subject minutes needs set.
Has set is singular. The plural subject minutes needs set.

items.explain:
The subject is minutes, which is plural. “Of a guest’s stay” is a prepositional phrase and does not change the subject. A plural subject needs a plural verb: minutes … set.

“Sets,” “is setting,” and “has set” are singular forms that wrongly agree with “stay.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the training manual. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Research on customer service shows that a warm greeting can {{0}} how guests feel about everything that follows, from the room to the restaurant.”

options: effect
affect
affects
effects
why: Effect is usually a noun meaning "a result." After "can," the sentence needs the verb meaning "to influence": affect.
Affects has an -s, but after the helping verb "can" use the base form: affect.
Effects is a noun (or an -s verb meaning "to bring about"). After "can," use the base verb affect.

items.explain:
The sentence needs a verb meaning “to influence.” That verb is affect. After the helping verb “can,” use the base form with no -s.

“Effect” is usually a noun meaning “a result,” and “affects” and “effects” cannot follow “can.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the training manual. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Greet each guest within ten seconds of {{0}} you are helping someone else, make eye contact and say that you will be right with them.”

options: arrival, if
arrival if
arrival. If
arrival; and if
why: A comma alone joins two complete sentences, creating a comma splice. End the first command with a period: arrival. If
No punctuation runs two sentences together. The first command ends at "arrival," so use a period.
A semicolon should not be followed by "and" here. The two commands are separate sentences, so use a period.

items.explain:
This passage contains two complete thoughts: a command (“Greet each guest within ten seconds of arrival”) and a second command with its own condition (“If you are helping someone else, make eye contact …”). Separating them with a period, arrival. If, makes two correct sentences.

A comma alone creates a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and a semicolon should not be followed by “and” here.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the training manual. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Before you hand over any keys, confirm the guest’s name, the number of nights, and {{0}}.”

options: checking the room type
to check the room type
that you checked the room type
the room type
why: Checking is a verb form, but the other list items are noun phrases ("the guest's name," "the number of nights"). Use the room type.
To check is an infinitive, which breaks the pattern of noun phrases. Use the room type.
That you checked is a clause, which breaks the parallel list of noun phrases. Use the room type.

items.explain:
Items in a list should have the same grammatical form. The first two items are noun phrases (“the guest’s name,” “the number of nights”), so the third should be a noun phrase too: the room type.

“Checking,” “to check,” and “that you checked” break the pattern.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the training manual. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“After swiping each card through the encoder, {{0}}.”

options: the desk reader should test it
you should test it on the desk reader
it should be tested on the desk reader
the card is tested on the desk reader
why: This makes the desk reader appear to do the swiping, a dangling modifier. The person who swipes, you, must come right after the comma.
"It" (the card) cannot swipe itself, so the opening phrase dangles. Name the person who swipes: you.
The card cannot swipe itself, so the opening phrase dangles. The subject after the comma must be you.

items.explain:
The opening phrase “After swiping each card through the encoder” must describe whoever does the swiping. The person swiping is the desk agent, so the sentence must name that person right after the comma: you should test it on the desk reader.

The other choices make the desk reader, “it,” or the card appear to do the swiping, which creates a dangling modifier.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the training manual. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Each card has {{0}} own expiration time, which is set automatically to noon on the checkout date.”

options: it’s
its
its’
their
why: It's means "it is"; "has it is own expiration time" makes no sense. The possessive is its.
Its' is never correct. The possessive of it has no apostrophe: its.
Their is plural, but "each card" is singular. Use its.

items.explain:
The possessive form of “it” is its, with no apostrophe. The card owns the expiration time.

“It’s” means “it is,” “its’” is never correct, and “their” is plural, but “each card” is singular.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the training manual. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Most guests check in without any problems. {{0}}, you will sometimes meet a guest whose room is not ready.”

options: Therefore
For example
However
Similarly
why: Therefore signals a result, but a room that is not ready does not result from smooth check-ins. The sentences contrast, so use However.
For example would introduce an example of smooth check-ins, but the second sentence describes a problem. Use However.
Similarly signals a comparison, but the two sentences contrast. Use However.

items.explain:
The second sentence contrasts with the first: most check-ins go smoothly, but some do not. However signals that contrast.

“Therefore” signals a result, “For example” introduces an example of the same idea, and “Similarly” signals a comparison. A room that is not ready is not a result or an example of check-ins going smoothly.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the training manual. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Beginning this {{0}} may also request a late checkout of 2 p.m. at no charge.”

options: Spring, guests who belong to Mesa Rewards
spring, guests who belong to Mesa Rewards
spring, guests who belong to mesa rewards
Spring, Guests who belong to Mesa Rewards
why: Seasons are common nouns, so spring should be lowercase.
Mesa Rewards is the name of a specific program, so both words must be capitalized.
Spring should be lowercase, and Guests is a common noun in the middle of the sentence, so it should be lowercase too.

items.explain: Names of seasons are common nouns and are not capitalized, so write spring. “Mesa Rewards” is the name of a specific program, a proper noun, so both words are capitalized. “Guests” is a common noun in the middle of the sentence and stays lowercase.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the training manual. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“If you are unsure how to handle any situation during check-in, ask the shift supervisor or {{0}}.”

options: I
myself
me
mine
why: I is a subject pronoun, but the word is an object of "ask." Test it: "ask I" is wrong; "ask me" is right.
Myself is used only when the subject is also "I." The subject here is the reader, so use me.
Mine is possessive. The object of "ask" needs the object pronoun me.

items.explain:
The pronoun is an object of the verb “ask,” so it must be in the object case: me. Test it by removing the other person: “ask me,” not “ask I.”

“Myself” is used only when the subject is also “I,” and “mine” shows possession.

essay.prompt:
The articles present arguments from a supporter and a critic of town programs that pay homeowners to replace grass lawns with native plants.

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Type your response in the box. This task may require approximately 45 minutes to complete.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Last week, a refrigeration failure at our Dayton distribution center {{0}} us to cancel more than 4,000 deliveries scheduled for March 9 through March 13.”

options: forces
will force
forced
has been forcing
why: Forces is present tense, but "Last week" places the action in the past. Use forced.
Will force is future tense, but the failure already happened last week.
Has been forcing describes something still going on. The failure was a completed event last week: forced.

items.explain:
“Last week” places the action in the completed past, so the simple past tense forced is correct.

“Forces” is present, “will force” is future, and “has been forcing” describes something still going on.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“We know that many of you were counting on those meals to feed {{0}} families, and we are truly sorry.”

options: there
their
they’re
there’s
why: There refers to a place. The families belong to the customers, so use the possessive their.
They're means "they are"; "feed they are families" makes no sense. Use their.
There's means "there is." The sentence needs the possessive their.

items.explain:
The families belong to the customers, so the possessive pronoun their is correct.

“There” refers to a place, “they’re” means “they are,” and “there’s” means “there is.”

items.prompt:
The writer wants to add a sentence right after “We did not ship any of the affected boxes.” Which choice is a complete, correctly written sentence?

{{0}}

options: Because we would never send food that might not be safe.
Which we would never do with food that might not be safe.
Not wanting to send food that might not be safe.
We would never send food that might not be safe.
why: This begins with "Because," making it a dependent clause with no main clause. It is a fragment.
This begins with "Which," making it a relative clause that cannot stand alone. It is a fragment.
"Not wanting…" is a phrase with no subject or main verb. It is a fragment.

items.explain:
Only We would never send food that might not be safe. is a complete sentence, with a subject (“We”) and a main verb (“would send”) expressing a complete thought.

The choice beginning with “Because” is a dependent clause, the one beginning with “Which” is a relative clause, and “Not wanting …” is a phrase with no main verb. All three are fragments when they stand alone.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Neither the delay nor the canceled orders {{0}} the standard you deserve from us, and we are taking responsibility for both.”

options: reflects
reflect
is reflecting
has reflected
why: Reflects agrees with "failure," but with neither … nor the verb agrees with the closer subject, "orders," which is plural. Use reflect.
Is reflecting is singular. The closer subject, "orders," is plural, so use reflect.
Has reflected is singular. The closer subject, "orders," is plural, so use reflect.

items.explain:
When two subjects are joined by neither … nor, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. The closer subject is “orders,” which is plural, so the verb is reflect.

“Reflects,” “is reflecting,” and “has reflected” are singular forms that wrongly agree with “failure.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Every affected customer will receive a credit for the full value of last {{0}} box, including shipping.”

options: weeks
weeks’
week’s
weeks’s
why: Weeks is a plural with no apostrophe, so it shows no possession. The box belongs to one week: week's.
Weeks' is plural possessive, meaning more than one week. "Last week" is one week: week's.
Weeks's is never a correct form. Use the singular possessive: week's.

items.explain:
The box belongs to one week (“last week”), so the singular possessive week’s is correct.

“Weeks” is a plural with no possession, “weeks’” would mean more than one week, and “weeks’s” is never correct.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“We have also installed a backup cooling system that can take over in less {{0}} five minutes if the main system fails again.”

options: then
than
that
then in
why: Then refers to time or sequence. A comparison such as "less than five minutes" uses than.
That does not complete a comparison. Use than.
"Then in" refers to time and adds an extra word. The comparison needs than.

items.explain:
Than is used to make comparisons (“less than five minutes”).

“Then” refers to time or sequence, and “that” does not complete a comparison.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“We are grateful for your {{0}} give us the chance to earn back your trust.”

options: patience, we hope you will
patience, and we hope you will
patience and, we hope you will
patience; and we hope you will
why: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice. Add a coordinating conjunction: patience, and we hope.
The comma belongs before "and," not after it. Write: patience, and we hope.
A semicolon is not used before "and" in a simple compound sentence like this. Use a comma before "and."

items.explain:
The sentence joins two independent clauses (“We are grateful for your patience” and “we hope you will give us the chance …”). The correct way to join them is a comma plus a coordinating conjunction: patience, and we hope you will.

A comma alone creates a comma splice. A comma placed after “and” is in the wrong spot, and a semicolon is not used before “and” in a simple compound sentence like this.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: The Richter scale remains the most accurate way to measure earthquakes of every size.
Scientific methods for describing earthquakes have improved over time, and magnitude and intensity each answer a different question about an earthquake.
Soft soil is the main reason that some earthquakes cause more damage than others.
Members of the public now measure earthquakes more accurately than scientists can.
items.explain:
The passage traces the history of measurement from seismometers (paragraph 2) to the Richter scale (paragraphs 3–4) to moment magnitude (paragraph 5), then explains that intensity measures something different from magnitude (paragraphs 6–7) and why accurate numbers matter (paragraph 8).

Paragraph 5 says moment magnitude has replaced the Richter scale for most measurements. Soft soil is one detail in paragraph 6, and public reports add intensity information; they do not replace scientists’ measurements.
why: Paragraph 5 says moment magnitude has replaced the Richter scale for most measurements because Richter underestimated large earthquakes.
Soft soil is one detail in paragraph 6, not the main idea of the whole passage.
Paragraph 7 says public reports add intensity information; they do not replace scientists' measurements.

items.prompt: In paragraph 3, the author says Richter made his scale “logarithmic.” Based on the paragraph, what does this word mean?
options: Each whole-number step adds the same fixed amount of shaking.
The scale uses Roman numerals instead of ordinary numbers.
The scale is based on reports from people who felt the earthquake.
Each whole-number step multiplies the measured amount by a set factor.
items.explain:
The author explains the word right after the colon: “each increase of one whole number represents a tenfold increase in the amplitude.” Going up one step multiplies the amplitude by 10, so a logarithmic scale grows by multiplying.

Equal added steps would describe an ordinary scale. Roman numerals and public reports belong to the intensity scale in paragraphs 6–7.
why: Equal added steps describe an ordinary scale. Paragraph 3 says each step is a "tenfold increase," which means multiplying.
Roman numerals belong to the Mercalli intensity scale in paragraph 6, not the Richter scale.
Reports from people who felt the shaking describe intensity (paragraphs 6–7), not Richter's logarithmic scale.

items.prompt: Using the information in paragraph 3, estimate how the energy released by a magnitude 8 earthquake compares with the energy released by a magnitude 5 earthquake.
options: about 96 times as much
about 1,000 times as much
about 3,000 times as much
about 33,000 times as much
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 says each one-step increase means “about 32 times more energy,” and its example shows that two steps multiply: magnitude 6 releases “roughly 1,000 times” the energy of magnitude 4 (32 × 32 = 1,024). From magnitude 5 to 8 is three steps: 32 × 32 × 32 = 32,768, or about 33,000 times as much energy.

About 1,000 times is the change in wave amplitude over three steps (10 × 10 × 10), not energy. About 96 times adds 32 + 32 + 32 instead of multiplying, and about 3,000 times multiplies 1,000 by the number of steps.
why: You added 32 three times (32 + 32 + 32). Each step multiplies the energy by 32, so three steps give 32 × 32 × 32 ≈ 33,000.
About 1,000 is the change in wave amplitude over three steps (10 × 10 × 10), not energy. Energy grows by about 32 each step.
You multiplied 1,000 by 3. The 1,000 covers two steps; the third step multiplies again by 32: 1,024 × 32 ≈ 33,000.

items.prompt: Paragraph 4 is shown below. Click the sentence that explains why the Richter method gave numbers that were too low for the largest earthquakes.
spans: The Richter scale was a breakthrough, but it had limits.
It was designed for earthquakes in Southern California, measured on one kind of instrument at fairly close distances.
More importantly, it did not work well for the largest earthquakes.
Above about magnitude 7, the method began to underestimate an earthquake’s size, because the waves it measured stopped growing as quickly as the earthquakes themselves did.
As a result, two very large earthquakes could receive similar Richter numbers even if one was far more powerful than the other.
items.explain:
This sentence gives the cause: the method underestimated size “because the waves it measured stopped growing as quickly as the earthquakes themselves did.”

The sentence before it states only that the method “did not work well,” and the last sentence describes the result (similar numbers for very different earthquakes), not the reason.
items.why: A common wrong click is "More importantly, it did not work well for the largest earthquakes," which states the problem but not the cause. The reason is in the next sentence: the waves it measured "stopped growing as quickly as the earthquakes themselves did."

items.prompt: According to paragraph 5, why does moment magnitude work for earthquakes of every size?
options: It is based on the physical size of the earthquake rather than on the height of a single recorded wave.
It uses many more seismometers than the Richter scale did.
It measures only earthquakes in Southern California.
It relies on reports from people who felt the shaking.
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 says moment magnitude is based on “the physical size of the earthquake itself” (rock stiffness, area of the fault that slipped, and distance moved), and “Because it measures the event directly rather than one of its effects, moment magnitude works for earthquakes of every size.”

The passage does not link the number of seismometers to this advantage. Being limited to Southern California was a weakness of the Richter scale, and public reports measure intensity, not magnitude.
why: The passage never links the number of seismometers to this advantage. Paragraph 5 says it works because it "measures the event directly."
Being limited to Southern California was a weakness of the Richter scale (paragraph 4); paragraph 5 says moment magnitude works "anywhere in the world."
Public reports measure intensity (paragraph 7), not magnitude.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, decide whether each statement describes magnitude or intensity. Drag each statement into the correct box.
choices: has a single value for each earthquake
can differ from town to town during the same earthquake
can be calculated from how far the two sides of a fault moved
can be estimated from reports submitted by the public
items.explain:
Magnitude: “A single earthquake has one magnitude” (paragraph 6), and moment magnitude is based partly on “how far the two sides of the fault moved” (paragraph 5).

Intensity: It “is written in Roman numerals” and produces “many intensity values” for one earthquake (paragraph 6), and the “Did You Feel It?” survey gathers “intensity information” from the public (paragraph 7).
items.why: The most common error is putting "can be estimated from reports submitted by the public" under magnitude. Paragraph 7 says the "Did You Feel It?" survey gathers intensity information; magnitude is one value per earthquake based on the fault's physical movement.

items.prompt: Which limitations of the original Richter scale does the passage describe? Select two answers.
options: It was designed for one region, one type of instrument, and fairly close distances.
It could not record earthquakes smaller than magnitude 4.
It underestimated the size of very large earthquakes.
It depended on people reporting what they felt.
It used Roman numerals that were difficult to compare.
items.explain:
Paragraph 4 lists both limitations: the scale “was designed for earthquakes in Southern California, measured on one kind of instrument at fairly close distances,” and “Above about magnitude 7, the method began to underestimate an earthquake’s size.”

The passage never mentions a lower limit on small earthquakes. Public reports and Roman numerals belong to the intensity scale, not the Richter scale.
why: The passage never mentions a lower limit for small earthquakes. Its stated problem is with the largest ones.
Reports from people who felt shaking describe the intensity scale (paragraphs 6–7), not the Richter scale.
Roman numerals belong to the Mercalli intensity scale (paragraph 6), not the Richter scale.

items.prompt: Two towns are the same distance from the source of an earthquake. Residents of one town report much stronger shaking than residents of the other. Based on paragraph 6, which explanation is most likely?
options: The earthquake had a higher magnitude in one town than in the other.
One town is built on loose, soft soil, and the other is built on solid rock.
One town used the Richter scale and the other used moment magnitude.
Fewer residents in one town completed the online survey.
items.explain:
Paragraph 6 explains that “loose, soft soil can make shaking stronger than it is on solid rock at the same distance.” That fits two towns at the same distance reporting different shaking.

An earthquake has only one magnitude, so it cannot be higher in one town. The choice of magnitude scale does not change how the ground shakes, and the number of survey responses does not change how strong the shaking felt to those who did respond.
why: Paragraph 6 says "A single earthquake has one magnitude," so it cannot be higher in one town.
Which scale is used to describe an earthquake does not change how strongly the ground shakes.
The number of survey responses does not change how strong the shaking was for those who felt it.

items.prompt: According to the FAQ, in what order do these steps happen when a customer requests a refund instead of a credit? Drag each step into the correct position.
choices: See the refund on a payment statement
Select the canceled box in Order History
items.explain: The numbered list gives the order: (1) log in, (2) open Order History and select the canceled box, (3) click Request Refund, and (4) watch for the confirmation email. The FAQ then says refunds appear on the statement “within 5 to 7 business days after you receive the confirmation email,” so seeing the refund comes last.
items.why: The most common error is putting "See the refund on a payment statement" before the confirmation email. The FAQ says refunds appear "within 5 to 7 business days after you receive the confirmation email," so seeing the refund is last.

items.prompt: A customer’s canceled box cost $72, including shipping. Her next box costs $60. According to the FAQ, what will happen?
options: The $72 credit will pay for her next box, and the remaining $12 will be applied to a later order.
She will receive a $12 refund to her original payment method.
She must pay $60 for her next box and use the credit on a later order.
The remaining $12 will expire when her next box is delivered.
items.explain:
The FAQ says the credit “is applied automatically to your next box,” and if it is larger than that box’s price, “the remaining balance carries over to your following orders until it is used up.” $72 − $60 = $12 carries over.

A refund happens only if she requests one or cancels her subscription. The credit is used on the next box, not saved, and credits expire after 90 days, not when a box is delivered.
why: A refund happens only if she requests one or cancels her subscription. Otherwise the leftover $12 "carries over to your following orders."
The FAQ says the credit "is applied automatically to your next box," so she will not pay $60 for it.
Credits expire 90 days after they are issued, not when a box is delivered. The leftover $12 carries over.

items.prompt: A customer whose box was canceled ended her Fieldstone subscription on March 15. According to the FAQ, what should she do to get her money back?
options: Request a refund through Order History by March 31.
Resume her subscription so the credit can be applied.
Nothing; the value of her canceled box will be refunded automatically by March 31.
Use the Report a Problem button within 7 days.
items.explain:
The FAQ answers this directly: for customers who canceled their subscription, “we will automatically refund the value of your canceled box to your original payment method by March 31. No action is needed.”

The Request Refund steps are for customers who still have a subscription and prefer a refund to a credit. The Report a Problem button is for boxes that arrived with damaged or missing items.
why: The Request Refund steps are for customers who still have a subscription. For canceled subscriptions, the FAQ says the refund is automatic and "No action is needed."
She does not need to resume. The FAQ says canceled subscribers are refunded automatically by March 31.
Report a Problem is for boxes that arrived with damaged or missing items, not for canceled boxes.

items.prompt: On March 22, a customer requests a refund for his canceled box. Later he notices that his account credit for that box is gone. Based on the FAQ, what is the best explanation?
options: His credit expired because he did not use it within 90 days.
The credit was removed because he chose a refund for the same box.
His request was too late, so both the credit and the refund were canceled.
Customers who skipped that week do not receive credits.
items.explain:
The FAQ states, “When you request a refund, the credit for that box is removed from your account. You cannot receive both a credit and a refund for the same box.” He chose the refund, so the credit was removed.

Only a few days have passed since credits were issued by March 20, far less than 90 days. March 22 is before the March 31 deadline, and his box was canceled by Fieldstone, so he did not skip that week.
why: Credits were issued by March 20, so only a few days have passed, far less than 90.
March 22 is before the March 31 refund deadline, so the request was on time.
His box was canceled by Fieldstone, so he did not skip that week; the skip rule does not apply.

items.prompt: Which customers are eligible for the missed delivery credit? Select two answers.
options: a customer whose box scheduled for March 11 was canceled by Fieldstone
a customer who chose to skip deliveries for the week of March 9
a customer whose box arrived on March 10 with a broken jar of sauce
a customer whose box scheduled for March 13 was canceled by Fieldstone
a customer whose box was scheduled for March 17
items.explain:
The FAQ says eligible customers had a box “scheduled for delivery between March 9 and March 13” that “was canceled by Fieldstone.” Boxes scheduled for March 11 and March 13 and canceled by Fieldstone both qualify.

Customers who skipped that week “are not eligible.” A box that arrived damaged is handled with the Report a Problem button, not this credit, and March 17 is outside the March 9–13 window.
why: The FAQ says customers who chose to skip that week "are not eligible."
Boxes delivered that week are "not part of this credit"; damaged items are handled with the Report a Problem button.
March 17 is outside the March 9–13 window, so this box is not covered.

items.prompt: How does the FAQ add to the information in Fieldstone’s letter to customers (the earlier passage)?
options: It explains why the refrigeration failure happened at the Dayton center.
It announces a new backup cooling system for the distribution center.
It changes the date by which credits will be added to customers’ accounts.
It tells customers that they may choose a refund instead of the automatic credit and explains how to request one.
items.explain:
The letter says only that every affected customer “will receive a credit” that “will appear in your account automatically by March 20.” The FAQ keeps that same date but adds a new option, a refund to the original payment method, with step-by-step instructions and a March 31 deadline.

The backup cooling system is mentioned only in the letter. Neither document explains the cause of the failure, and both give the same March 20 date for credits.
why: Neither document explains why the refrigeration failure happened.
The backup cooling system is announced in the letter, not the FAQ.
Both documents give the same date, March 20, for credits.
